issues.legal_issue: A previously accepted and judicially determined right of legal representatives to continue a pending mining-lease application cannot be reopened in later proceedings merely because a subsequent decision changes the interpretation of the governing law.
material_facts: The legal representatives were permitted to pursue the deceased applicant’s mining-lease application, and the competing applicant participated in proceedings concerning their substitution.

The competing applicant did not challenge their standing during subsequent proceedings before the Central Government and did not challenge a later High Court judgment that again proceeded on the basis that they could pursue the application.
The competing applicant later challenged the grant of the lease, relying on a subsequent Supreme Court decision concerning the applicable rule.
The High Court declined to reopen the legal representatives’ standing, and the Supreme Court found that conclusion justified in light of the litigation history between the parties.
issues.conclusion: The legal representatives’ standing to pursue the application could not be reopened in the later proceedings; the High Court was entitled to decline relief based on the prior litigation history and finality between the parties.
issues.legal_principle: A judicial determination by a competent court may bind the parties even if it is erroneous; a subsequent change or clarification in law does not ordinarily unsettle a matter that has become final between them. The Court relied on Mohanlal Goenka v. Benoy Kishna Mukherjee and State of West Bengal v. Hemant Kumar Bhattacharjee. It also noted that the later decision in Saligram Khirwal v. Union of India held that the relevant rule operated prospectively, but that decision did not reopen the matter concluded between these parties. Although strict res judicata may not apply to proceedings before the Central Government, a High Court exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 may consider the prior history between the parties in deciding whether to grant relief.

rule.if: later_challenge_to_heirs_lease_application and prior_final_locus_determination and appellant_accepted_heirs_locus and later_change_in_legal_interpretation

predicates.later_challenge_to_heirs_lease_applicati: A party brings a later proceeding challenging the ability of legal representatives to continue a pending mining-lease application.
predicates.prior_final_locus_determination: A competent court previously determined, or proceeded on the basis, that the legal representatives could pursue the application.
predicates.appellant_accepted_heirs_locus: The challenging party participated in earlier proceedings concerning the legal representatives’ standing and did not challenge that standing when it could do so.
predicates.later_change_in_legal_interpretation: A later decision changes or clarifies the interpretation of law relevant to the legal representatives’ ability to pursue the application.

issues.definition: When a party later challenges legal representatives’ ability to pursue an application after that ability has been finally determined and accepted between the parties, a later change in legal interpretation does not permit the issue to be reopened.

issues.legal_issue: A government decision following a hearing by the government as an institution is not invalid merely because an official other than the hearing officer signs or communicates the resulting order.
material_facts: The High Court directed the Central Government to hear the competing applicants and decide the matter.
A Joint Secretary heard the parties, received their documents and submissions, and prepared a detailed note containing the proposed decision.
The note was approved by the Secretary and the Minister, and the resulting order substantially reproduced the note.
A Deputy Secretary signed the order, and the record showed that the signature served to communicate the Central Government’s approval.
issues.conclusion: The hearing by the Central Government satisfied the requirement of natural justice; the different official’s signing and communication of the order did not make the decision legally or procedurally infirm.
issues.legal_principle: A decision with adverse civil consequences must be made after hearing the affected parties, but, absent a contrary statutory direction, an administrative body may act through its ordinary institutional procedures and rely on its officials to obtain and present materials. The Court relied on Local Government Board v. Arlidge, as approved in Pradyat Kumar Bose v. The Hon’ble the Chief Justice of Calcutta High Court, and considered the principles of natural justice also reflected in Automotive Tyre Manufacturers Association v. Designated Authority.

rule.if: government_lease_decision_after_remand and affected_parties_heard_by_government and hearing_officer_prepared_decision_record and decision_approved_through_government_process and different_official_only_signed_or_communicated

predicates.government_lease_decision_after_remand: A government decides competing claims to a lease after a court has sent the matter back for a hearing and fresh decision.
predicates.affected_parties_heard_by_government: The affected competing parties are given an opportunity to present their submissions and materials to the government.
predicates.hearing_officer_prepared_decision_record: The official who heard the parties prepares a record or recommendation addressing the matter.
predicates.decision_approved_through_government_pro: The recommendation is considered and approved through the government’s decision-making process.
predicates.different_official_only_signed_or_commun: An official other than the hearing officer signs or communicates the order without being the person who decided the matter.

issues.definition: When affected parties are heard by the government, the hearing officer prepares the decision record, and the government approves the decision through its process, a different official may sign or communicate the order without defeating natural justice.

issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of an administrative or quasi-judicial lease decision is confined to legality and the decision-making process and does not permit a court to reweigh the merits where the decision is supported by the record and the process is not shown to be unlawful or irrational.
material_facts: The Central Government considered material submitted by the State Government and by the competing applicants, and additional reports obtained from the Indian Bureau of Mines were made available to the parties.
The parties were permitted to submit documents and written arguments, and the hearing officer prepared a detailed note that was approved through the government’s decision-making process.
The High Court examined the record and found no flaw in the decision-making process; the Supreme Court found no basis to disturb that conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The High Court committed no error in upholding the government’s decision, and the Supreme Court would not interfere with it on judicial review.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review of administrative and quasi-judicial action addresses errors of law, breach of natural justice, irrationality, abuse of power, and decisions unsupported by evidence; it is not an appeal on the merits. A court may intervene where the decision-making authority exceeds its powers, commits an error of law, breaches natural justice, reaches a decision no reasonable tribunal would reach, or abuses its powers. The Court relied on Tata Cellular v. Union of India.

predicates.judicial_review_of_administrative_lease_: A party asks a court to review a government’s administrative or quasi-judicial decision on competing lease claims.
predicates.parties_received_opportunity_to_submit_m: The affected parties were allowed to provide documents and submissions relevant to the decision.
predicates.decision_based_on_record: The government considered material in the record when reaching its decision.
predicates.no_proven_process_or_legality_defect: The reviewing court finds no established error of law, breach of natural justice, irrationality, abuse of power, or absence of evidentiary support.

issues.definition: When judicial review is sought, the parties had an opportunity to submit material, the decision rests on the record, and no reviewable defect is established, the court does not interfere with the government’s decision.
